UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                          )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                               )                       Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                          )

                       COMMENTS AND LIMITED PROTEST OF
                 SOUTHERN MARYLAND ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC.

         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (the “Commission”) 1 and in accordance with the Commission’s

Combined Notice of Filings notice issued August 13, 2026, Southern Maryland Electric

Cooperative, Inc. (“SMECO”) 2 respectfully submits this Comments and Limited Protest regarding

the filing that PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) submitted in the above-captioned docket on

August 13, 2026 (the “IRAS Filing”). 3


         PJM proposes revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the

Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish a new

“Interim Resource Adequacy Service” (“IRAS”) and an associated “Large Load Registry.” As

proposed by PJM, IRAS is a supplemental capacity product through which Eligible New Large

Loads may be directed by the Electric Distributor to reduce their load in response to an Interim

Resource Adequacy Service Action called by PJM. 4




1
   18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025).
2
  SMECO is an electric distribution cooperative organized under the laws of the State of Maryland and is an “Electric
Distributor,” as that term is defined in the PJM Amended and Restated Operating Agreement (“Operating
Agreement” or “OA”), serving retail customers in Southern Maryland. In this proceeding, SMECO submitted, and
the Commission accepted a (doc-less) motion to intervene on August 25, 2026.
3
  Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability, Transmittal Letter of
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (August 13, 2026) (“IRAS Filing”).
4
  IRAS Filing at 74.


                                                         1
         Specifically, beginning with the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, IRAS would allow New Large

Loads to interconnect without first securing capacity to cover their full demand, subject to a

condition: PJM may direct the Electric Distributor serving such a load to reduce an aggregate

quantity of that load -- ahead of PJM’s existing Pre-Emergency Load Management Reductions --

when PJM determines that available real-time supply may be insufficient to maintain required

reserves. 5


        SMECO’s comments and limited protest address certain aspects of the IRAS Filing,

including whether the real-time Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action mechanism that Mr.

Christopher Pilong’s affidavit describes will operate as PJM intends without exposing Electric

Distributors’ core native load to curtailment, and further aspects in which Electric Distributors are

assigned new operational, data-reporting, compensation-administration responsibilities and

exposure to payments and default allocations for payments owed by other entities under PJM’s

proposed billing indemnification provision.


I. INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

        PJM’s IRAS proposal responds to the same capacity shortfall underlying PJM’s separate

Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) filing in Docket No. ER26-3380 – namely, that the

2028/2029 Delivery Year Base Residual Auction cleared 6,831.3 MW short of the PJM Region

Reliability Requirement, a shortfall PJM attributes in substantial part to the rapid interconnection

of large loads, including data centers. 6 Where the RBP is a one-time capacity procurement, IRAS

is a standing framework – i.e., it permits New Large Loads to connect to the PJM system ahead of


5
 IRAS Filing at 74–77.
6
 IRAS Filing at 21 (describing the 2028/2029 Delivery Year Base Residual Auction shortfall); see also Reliability
Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-
3380-000, PJM Transmittal Letter at 2 (July 31, 2026).


                                                         2
 securing their own capacity, in exchange for exposing the uncovered portion of that load to

curtailment before PJM calls on Pre-Emergency Load Management Reductions. 7


             However, the IRAS Filing assigns Electric Distributors a series of new duties -- to execute

IRAS Action directives, to help build and validate a data registry, to coordinate retail deployment

of load reductions, and to implement a wholesale compensation program -- while leaving several

design questions either unresolved or deferred to future PJM Manual revisions. SMECO focuses

on the following issues:


         •    New duties that proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4 impose on Electric Distributors,
              certain of go beyond the metering, data-reporting, and physical emergency-response
              functions historically assigned to Electric Distributors under the PJM Operating
              Agreement (“OA”).

         •    A real-time Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action that directs an Electric
              Distributor to reduce its full, pre-assigned aggregate MW quantity without regard to
              whether the underlying New Large Load is actually energized and taking service, risking
              curtailment of the Electric Distributor’s existing, non-Large-Load native customers.

         •    A billing indemnification provision 8 that assigns Electric Distributors all of the risk that
              another entity -- potentially an LSE with which the Electric Distributor has no affiliation
              -- fails to pay IRAS compensation it owes, with no PJM-level credit support of any kind.

         •    Mechanics of the proposed Large Load Registry’s data-reporting mandate on Electric
              Distributors, that PJM proposes to defer to PJM Manual revisions that have not yet been
              drafted; PJM’s proposal also identifies no mechanism for Electric Distributors to recover
              the costs of Large Load Registry compliance.

II. BACKGROUND

             PJM submitted the IRAS Filing on August 13, 2026, requesting that the Commission act

by no later than October 12, 2026, so that PJM may begin implementing the Large Load Registry




7
    IRAS Filing at 74–77.
8
     Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section X(b)(iii)


                                                           3
 and the other proposed Tariff and RAA revisions on that date. IRAS itself would not become

available until the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, beginning June 1, 2027. 9


         PJM proposes to define “Large Load” as end-use customer load with a cumulative peak of

50 MW or greater at a single electrical site, including affiliated load facilities within a one-mile

radius under specified configurations. 10 A “New Large Load” is a Large Load (or incremental load

at an existing site) that enters service after June 1, 2027, 11 and an “Eligible New Large Load” is a

New Large Load that has not entered into a “Bring Your Own New Capacity” (“BYONC”)

arrangement or has not been allocated UCAP MW through the RBP. 12


         IRAS is triggered when PJM determines that available economic real-time supply may not

be sufficient to maintain required reserves or applicable Interconnection Reliability Operating

Limits. 13 In that circumstance, PJM may issue an “Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action”

directing the affected Electric Distributor to reduce an aggregate MW quantity of load -- based on

the zone/area’s pre-Delivery Year IRAS obligation -- before calling on existing Pre-Emergency

Load Management Reduction Actions. 14


         Notably, PJM will not itself identify which specific New Large Loads must reduce load;

that determination is left to the Electric Distributor, who in coordination with the relevant state

and/or Electric Retail Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”), LSEs, and LSE customers, make that

specific as to which New Large Loads would need to be reduced; rather, it will be based on the

aggregate MW of reduction available from the Eligible New Large Loads in the zone/area.” 16


         Compensation for IRAS load reductions is set at a wholesale rate of up to 50% of the

existing Non-Performance Charge Rate, but the rate can be reduced -- including to zero -- if the

Eligible New Large Load elects a lower or no payment in its retail rate. 17 How that wholesale rate

reaches an Eligible New Large Load, and how (or whether) it is funded at the retail level, is left to

the Electric Distributor, in conjunction with the applicable state authority or RERRA. 18


         To administer both IRAS and the Large Load Registry, PJM’s proposal assigns Electric

Distributors four (4) duties under proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section III:


     •   Executing PJM’s Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action directives;

     •   Coordinating with PJM on Large Load Registry development, including by providing “any
         information or data the Electric Distributor believes appropriate to facilitate an accurate
         Large Load Registry;” 19

     •   Coordinating with the relevant state(s) or RERRA(s), LSEs, and LSE customers to support
         “transparent, effective, and orderly deployment” of IRAS; 20 and

     •   Implementing the IRAS compensation program. 21

 III. COMMENTS.

A. PJM’s IRAS Proposal Assigns Significant New Electric Distributor Responsibilities.

         In its IRAS Filing, Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section III requires that Electric

Distributors “shall” fulfill four tasks:


     1. Execute IRAS Load Reductions. An Electric Distributor must “execute the Office of the
     Interconnection’s directives to implement Interim Resource Adequacy Service Actions.” 22

     SMECO does not object to this task, which is a natural extension of the Electric Distributor’s
     existing Emergency-response role.

     2. Build and validate the Large Load Registry. An Electric Distributor must “provide PJM
     with any information or data the Electric Distributor believes appropriate to facilitate an
     accurate Large Load Registry, including applicable state or RERRA retail tariff or contractual
     obligations,” and coordinate with PJM and the applicable Transmission Owner to “check the
     validity of the information provided.” 23

     This task goes beyond OA section 11.3.3(h)’s data-reporting obligation, which speaks to data
     “necessary or appropriate to implement or administer” the OA and RAA themselves -- not to
     serving as a validation source for a registry whose contents is built on information originating
     with LSEs or Large Loads that the Electric Distributor does not necessarily control. 24

     3. Identify which retail customers to curtail. An Electric Distributor must “coordinate, as
     appropriate, with the relevant state(s) or RERRA(s), individual [LSEs], and customers served
     by the [LSEs] in its zone/area to support transparent, effective, and orderly deployment” of
     IRAS. 25 PJM characterizes this function as “memorializing” existing practice, under which
     Electric Distributors already determine, consistent with state programs, which loads to reduce
     in response to a PJM directive. 26

     While PJM OA sections 11.3.3(c) and (e) require an Electric Distributor to maintain load-
     shedding capability and to “[s]hed connected load … and take such other coordination actions
     as may be necessary in accordance with the directions of the Office of the Interconnection in
     Emergencies” -- an operational, physical-curtailment obligation 27, PJM’s description of the
     coordination duty as a “memorialization” of past practice does not change that Electric

      Distributors are, for the first time, being asked to administer eligibility and curtailment-priority
     determinations under an entirely new service category.

     4. Implement the IRAS compensation program. An Electric Distributor must “implement
     [a] compensation program consistent with Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section X.” 28 It requires
     the Electric Distributor to administer, collect for, and disburse a PJM wholesale-rate-linked
     payment obligation.

IV. LIMITED PROTEST.

B. PJM’s Real-Time Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action Mechanism Does Not
Confirm That the New Large Load Underlying an Electric Distributor’s Assigned
Obligation Is Actually Energized or Online, Risking Curtailment of Core Native Load.

         The Affidavit of Christopher Pilong, submitted in support of the IRAS Filing, confirms

that the “[i]dentification of an IRAS requirement for each Electric Distributor’s zone/area

establishes the reliability obligation applicable to affected load,” 29 and that “the IRAS requirement

establishes an operational reliability resource available to PJM, which can be called upon when

actual system conditions indicate that the reliability need addressed by the IRAS requirement is

materializing.” 30


         Nothing in Mr. Pilong’s affidavit, however, ties PJM’s actual exercise of that authority in

real time to whether the New Large Load generating the obligation, in fact, is energized and taking

service. To the contrary, Mr. Pilong describes an Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action as a

directive to reduce a fixed, pre-set quantity of load at the Electric Distributor zone/area level,

determined without regard to real-time large-load operating status.


         Specifically, the MW quantity of IRAS assigned to a given zone/area is fixed “prior to the

start of each Delivery Year,” and thereafter is simply the figure “utilized by PJM Dispatch in their



28
   IRAS Filing at 27 (quoting proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section III(d)).
29
    Affidavit of Christopher Pilong para 21.
30
   Affidavit of Christopher Pilong para 22.


                                                         7
 system projections, alerts and actions.” 31 When PJM later calls an actual Interim Resource

Adequacy Service Action, Mr. Pilong explains that PJM Dispatchers “will direct Electric

Distributors to implement reductions in load up to, and capped at, the pre-Delivery Year IRAS

obligations they were assigned” -- the pre-set figure, not a real-time measure of the underlying

load’s actual consumption -- and that PJM “will not direct specific New Large Loads to reduce

load” but instead “will only direct load reduction of an aggregate MW IRAS within the zone or

area.” 32 The affidavit describes PJM Dispatchers calling, in an RTO-wide emergency, “for some

or all Electric Distributors to reduce load across the PJM RTO Region” based on “the maximum

IRAS amounts assigned to each Electric Distributor zone/area” -- again with no reference to

whether the New Large Load behind that assignment is actually in service. 33


         This is not a remote hypothetical. The New Large Loads whose lack of BYONC makes

them “Eligible” for IRAS treatment in the first place -- because, as described above, they have not

secured a BYONC arrangement and have not been allocated sufficient RBP UCAP MW34 -- are,

as a structural matter, disproportionately likely to be projects still working through

interconnection, construction, or commissioning, rather than loads already drawing their full

expected demand, if any demand at all based upon the state of project development.


         Mr. Pilong’s affidavit also confirms that an Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action

“prioritizes load reduction from those Electric Distributor zones/areas where New Large Loads

have not brought their own new capacity and do not have Allocated Reliability Backstop

   Affidavit of Christopher Pilong para 28.
32
   Affidavit of Christopher Pilong para 42.

 Procurement Unforced Capacity Megawatts … sufficient to cover their capacity needs” -- the same

under-covered load that defines Eligible New Large Load status in the first place. 35


            And, because an Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action need not be preceded by any

day-ahead alert -- Mr. Pilong acknowledges that “it is not a requirement that an Interim Resource

Adequacy Service Alert be issued prior to an Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action” 36 -- an

Electric Distributor may have no advance opportunity to flag that its assigned New Large Load is

not yet in service before PJM’s Action issues.


            If an Electric Distributor’s assigned New Large Load has not yet been energized -- or has

only begun a ramp or testing period well short of its expected draw -- at the time PJM issues an

Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action, the Electric Distributor will nonetheless receive a

directive to reduce its full pre-Delivery Year MW quantity. Because that New Large Load is not

consuming power to reduce, and because the Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action is

directed to the Electric Distributor’s zone/area as a whole rather than to any specific load, the

Electric Distributor’s only means of complying would be to curtail its core, non-Large-Load native

customers.


            That outcome is the opposite of what IRAS is meant to achieve and would adversely impact

SMECO’s ability to provide safe and reliable service on its electric distribution system to its

customer-members. SMECO respectfully requests that the Commission direct PJM to clarify:


            1.       Whether an Electric Distributor’s obligation under an Interim Resource Adequacy
                     Service Action is capped by the New Large Load MW actually energized and taking

                  service in its zone/area at the time of the Action, rather than by the full pre-Delivery
                 Year assigned quantity;

        2.       If clarification point #1 above is not capped as described, what safeguard, if any,
                 prevents an Electric Distributor from being directed to reduce more load than its
                 interconnected, energized New Large Load represents, such that the Electric
                 Distributor would be required to curtail core native load to comply; and

        3.       Whether PJM will commit to adjusting/suspending an Electric Distributor’s
                 assigned IRAS obligation when the underlying New Large Load’s in-service date
                 is delayed beyond what PJM assumed in setting the zone/area’s pre-Delivery Year
                 quantity.

C. The IRAS Filing’s Billing Indemnification Provision Shifts Compensation Default Risk
to Electric Distributors, Including for Payments Owed by Other Entities.

        The PJM Filing proposes “IRAS Compensation”, in which “Electric Distributors bear the

responsibility to implement the compensation scheme for New Large Loads that provide the IRAS

load reduction service.” 37 As noted above, PJM is proposing a rate for IRAS that is equal to 50%

of the Non-Performance Charge Rate. Given that the current RTO-wide Non-Performance Charge

Rate is approximately $2,278/MWh (for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year), a new large load that did

not arrange for new capacity would be compensated for curtailing at a rate of over $1,100/MWh.

However, proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section X(b)(iii) provides that “neither PJM nor the

PJM membership, generally, is financially responsible for any potential defaults that may arise in

association with the billing of” IRAS compensation.” 38 Under this provision, if a state-approved

rate requires collection of IRAS compensation from other LSEs, and an LSE does not pay as

required -- “whether billed directly by the Electric Distributor or by PJM upon request of the

Electric Distributor” -- “the default will not pass to the PJM membership,” and instead “any default

shall be assessed to the Electric Distributor.” 39

                                                         10
             PJM acknowledges that “in restructured states, the LSE may be an independent entity, not

affiliated with the Electric Distributor.” 40 Where that is so, an Electric Distributor directed to bill

(or to request that PJM bill) another LSE for IRAS compensation would bear the full risk of that

unaffiliated LSE’s non-payment, notwithstanding that the Electric Distributor has no ownership

relationship, and potentially no pre-existing commercial or credit relationship, with the paying

LSE. PJM’s proposal includes no mechanism -- no collateral requirement or no PJM-administered

mutualization -- to protect the Electric Distributor against that exposure. SMECO respectfully

requests that the Commission direct PJM to revise section X(b)(iii) to limit an Electric

Distributor’s exposure to such circumstances.


D. The Large Load Registry Rests on Key Details That PJM Proposes to Develop Only
After the Registry Takes Effect, With No Identified Cost-Recovery Mechanism.

            Proposed RAA, Schedule 11, section B.1(b) directs PJM to obtain Large Load Registry

information from Electric Distributors, and proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section III(b)

requires an Electric Distributor to supply “any information or data the Electric Distributor believes

appropriate to facilitate an accurate Large Load Registry, including applicable state or RERRA

retail tariff or contractual obligations.” 41 PJM’s proposes that its Large Load Registry will contain

the following information about each Large Load in the PJM Region:


       •    Eligible Customer/Network Customer for Large Load;
       •    Description of Large Load;
       •    Location(s) (Control Zone, Electric Distributor zone/area, where a zone/area is an area
            within a Zone for which the relevant Electric Distributor specifies a separate Obligation
            Peak Load MW value. A zone/area is a service area of an Electric Distributor that is a
            separately identifiable, geographic area bounded by wholesale metering);
       •    In-service date for each increment of load;
       •    Peak shaving adjustment value pursuant to a state program codified in state law and
            whether and how it meets the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-2;

      •   Delivery point / Point(s) of interconnection (include all if more than one);
     •   Peak load quantity (MW) and ramp schedule, if applicable;
     •   Telemetry specifications;
     •   BYONC quantity (MW) and ramp schedule, if applicable;
     •   Allocated RBP UCAP MW quantity (MW), if applicable;
     •   Backup generation (MW), including fuel type and relevant permitting limitations;
     •   Contracts or service agreements between the Large Load and the LSE;
     •   Points of contact at the applicable Transmission Owner, Electric Distributor, and Load
         Serving Entity;
     •   EMS B1/B2/B3 name (for the applicable Transmission Owner, Electric Distributor); and
         Additional details and contents as necessary, in accordance with the PJM Manuals. 42

         The IRAS Filing, however, defers the mechanics of this mandate to PJM Manual revisions

that have not yet been reviewed. For example, among other items deferred to later development,

PJM states that it “intends to develop provisions in its Manuals to implement the Large Load

Registry, as needed, including details about who may access the information and specific

safeguards in place to maintain the confidentiality of certain data.” 43


         Electric Distributors are thus asked to commit to an obligation whose scope, format, and

confidentiality protections will not be defined until after the Tariff and RAA revisions PJM

proposes in the IRAS filing take effect. 44 This timing is compounded by a liability concern PJM

raises. That is, submitters of Large Load Registry information are subject to the Commission’s

prohibition on untrue statements or material omissions under FPA Section 222 and 18 C.F.R. Part

1c, backed by civil penalties that can exceed $1.5 million per violation per day, and that “Sellers”

additionally owe a duty of candor to the Commission and to PJM under 18 C.F.R. § 35.41(b). 45

            However, much of the underlying data an Electric Distributor is asked to relay into the

Large Load Registry (see list above), will originate with the LSE serving the Large Load or with

the Large Load itself, neither of which the Electric Distributor necessarily controls or can

independently verify. 46 PJM’s IRAS Filing does not clarify the scope of an Electric Distributor’s

potential exposure under the above-noted anti-fraud and candor provisions for registry information

it receives from, and relays on behalf of, third parties.


       Finally, the IRAS Filing identifies no mechanism through which an Electric Distributor may

recover the costs (administrative and systems) of complying with the Large Load Registry’s data-

supply, validation, and coordination duties. SMECO respectfully requests that the Commission

direct PJM to (i) file the Manual provisions implementing the Large Load Registry’s data formats,

one-mile-site methodology, and confidentiality safeguards for review before -- not after -- the

Large Load Registry becomes effective; (ii) clarify the scope of an Electric Distributor’s potential

liability for registry information sourced from LSEs or Large Loads; and (iii) identify a mechanism

for Electric Distributors to recover the reasonable costs of Large Load Registry compliance.
